---
title: "From Raw Prices to a Clean Panel"
subtitle: "Download, parse, and turn prices into returns"
---



Every market example in this course runs on one small table: daily **returns**
for 14 stocks, spanning almost two decades.  This page shows where that table
comes from and how it's built — the download, the parse, and the one
transformation (prices → log-returns) that turns raw quotes into something we can
do statistics on.

---

## 1 · The Source and the Basket

The prices come from **Yahoo Finance**, pulled with the
[`yfinance`](https://github.com/ranaroussi/yfinance) library: daily
**split- and dividend-adjusted** closes from **2007 to 2025**.  That window is
deliberate — it straddles the **two great bank co-crashes** the course keeps
returning to: the 2008 global financial crisis and the 2020 COVID crash.

We keep a curated **14-stock basket** across five sectors, chosen so the
dependence lessons are visible to the naked eye: five banks that crash together,
three mega-cap tech names, energy, and defensive utilities/staples that march to
a different drum.

::: {#tbl-basket .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
meta = datasets.load_basket_meta()
print(meta.to_string(index=False))
```

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Why These 14?

The **sector** column is the story.  Banks (JPM, BAC, C, WFC, GS) share a risk
factor and move almost as one; utilities (DUK, SO) and staples (PG, KO) are
defensive and barely co-move with the banks.  That spread of behaviour is exactly
what makes correlation, co-crashes, and tail dependence *legible* later.

*(We use `GOOG` — Alphabet's Class C share — rather than `GOOGL`, because
Yahoo's `GOOGL` history only begins at the 2014 share-class split, while `GOOG`
runs continuously from 2004.)*
:::

## 2 · The Pipeline

The download script does three things: fetch the **adjusted** close panel for the
basket (`yfinance` returns it already wide, one column per ticker), drop days with
any missing quote, and convert prices to **log-returns**.  The committed script is
[`scripts/download_market_data.py`](../../scripts/download_market_data.py); its
core is just:

```python
# scripts/download_market_data.py (excerpt — runs once, needs network)
import yfinance as yf
raw    = yf.download(TICKERS, start="2007-01-01", end="2025-12-31",
                     auto_adjust=True)               # adjusted for splits/divs
prices = raw["Close"].dropna(how="any")              # wide price panel
rets   = np.log(prices / prices.shift(1)).dropna(how="any")   # log-returns
rets.to_csv("data/processed/returns_basket.csv")
```

The `auto_adjust=True` flag matters: it folds **dividends and splits** into the
price (e.g. Citigroup's 2011 1-for-10 reverse split), so a "return" reflects what
an investor actually earned — not an artificial jump on the split date.

We don't re-download at page-render time (CI has no network); the result is
committed as `data/processed/returns_basket.csv` and loaded with
`datasets.load_returns()`.

## 3 · Why Log-Returns?

A **return** answers "how much did one dollar grow today?"  The *original* number
is the **simple return** $P_t/P_{t-1} - 1$ — the everyday percentage change.  We
instead work with the *log* return $r_t = \log(P_t / P_{t-1})$.  The two are close
but not identical, and it's worth *seeing* the difference before trusting it.

::: {#cell-fig-simple-vs-log .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import matplotlib.dates as mdates

simple = np.exp(R) - 1                 # recover the original simple returns
name = "C"                             # Citigroup — the panel's most violent days
win = (R.index >= "2008-09-01") & (R.index <= "2009-04-30")

fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.8))
axL.plot(R.index[win], 100 * simple[name][win], color=plotting.COOL, lw=1.3,
         label=r"simple  $P_t/P_{t-1}-1$")
axL.plot(R.index[win], 100 * R[name][win], color=plotting.CRASH, lw=1.3,
         label=r"log  $\ln(P_t/P_{t-1})$")
axL.axhline(0, color=INK, lw=0.6)
axL.set_title("Citigroup, daily — through the GFC", fontsize=11)
axL.set_ylabel("return (%)"); axL.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False)
axL.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.MonthLocator(interval=2))
axL.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b %Y"))
despine(axL)

s_all = simple.to_numpy().ravel() * 100
l_all = R.to_numpy().ravel() * 100
axR.scatter(s_all, l_all, s=4, c=plotting.COOL, alpha=0.25, edgecolors="none")
lim = [s_all.min() - 2, s_all.max() + 2]
axR.plot(lim, lim, color=INK, lw=1.2, ls="--", label="log = simple")
axR.set_xlim(lim); axR.set_ylim(lim)
axR.set_title("Every day, every name", fontsize=11)
axR.set_xlabel("simple return (%)"); axR.set_ylabel("log return (%)")
axR.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper left"); despine(axR)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Left: Citigroup's simple and log returns day-by-day through the 2008–09 crisis — indistinguishable on ordinary days, parting only on the violent ones. Right: every day of every name. The two agree along the dashed line near the origin but bend away in the tails, where the log return is always the more stabilising of the two (it tames big gains and deepens big losses, symmetrising both).](01-downloading-and-parsing_files/figure-html/fig-simple-vs-log-output-1.png){#fig-simple-vs-log width=1185 height=441}
:::
:::


We prefer the log return for two reasons the picture hints at: it **adds up over
time** (a week's return is the sum of its days — no compounding bookkeeping), and
it's roughly **symmetric**, which keeps the statistics well-behaved.  The
additivity is the deeper one: a +50% gain followed by a −50% loss leaves you down
to 0.75 of where you started, and only the log returns record that honestly — they
sum to $\ln 1.5 + \ln 0.5 = -0.29 = \ln 0.75$, while the simple returns would
falsely net to zero.

Because they add up, we can run the transformation **backward** to recover a price
path from returns — a cumulative sum inside an exponential.  We don't ship prices,
so we reconstruct an illustrative path here (starting every name at 100) purely to
*see* what the returns encode.  The vertical axis is **logarithmic**: over 19
years Apple compounds more than 100-fold while Citigroup falls some 98%, a range
no linear axis can show at once.

::: {#cell-fig-price-paths .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
meta = datasets.load_basket_meta().set_index("ticker")
prices = 100 * np.exp(R.cumsum())            # P_t = 100 * exp(sum of log-returns)

sector_color = {
    "Banks": plotting.CRASH, "Tech": plotting.COOL, "Energy": "#b08968",
    "Utilities": plotting.PALETTE["green"], "Staples": plotting.PALETTE["purple"],
}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.6))
seen = set()
for t in prices.columns:
    sec = meta.loc[t, "sector"]
    ax.plot(prices.index, prices[t], color=sector_color[sec], lw=1.2, alpha=0.8,
            label=sec if sec not in seen else None)
    seen.add(sec)
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_ylabel("price (indexed to 100, log scale)"); ax.set_xlabel("date")
ax.set_title("Nineteen years, 14 names, coloured by sector", fontsize=12)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, ncol=5, loc="upper left")
despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Reconstructed price paths (each name indexed to 100 at the start, log scale), coloured by sector. The banks (red) plunge together in 2008 and again in 2020; tech compounds relentlessly; utilities and staples drift calmly through both crises. This is the cumulative story the daily returns table encodes.](01-downloading-and-parsing_files/figure-html/fig-price-paths-output-1.png){#fig-price-paths width=1064 height=537}
:::
:::


And the round-trip confirms the formula: re-deriving log-returns from the
reconstructed prices reproduces the original table exactly.

::: {#0b166b45 .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
back = np.log(prices / prices.shift(1)).dropna(how="any")
print(f"max |reconstructed return - original| = {np.abs(back - R.loc[back.index]).to_numpy().max():.2e}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
max |reconstructed return - original| = 6.52e-16
```
:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip}
## The Takeaway
One table, two views: the **returns** are what we do statistics on (stationary,
additive); the **prices** are the cumulative story they tell.  Everything in the
market chapters starts from `datasets.load_returns()`.
:::
